personality_voice.book_baseline: Across all seven books, book Harry's personality is defined by a layered cluster of interlocking traits: instinctive, reluctant bravery; fierce loyalty to those he loves; a dry, sardonic wit deployed as a coping mechanism; volcanic but shame-inducing anger that he is often unable to control; a persistent undercurrent of insecurity and self-doubt beneath the heroic surface; a powerful moral compass that makes him defy authority when he believes it is wrong; and a rich, self-interrogating interior monologue that constitutes a major dimension of his characterisation. In the early books (PS, CoS) this voice is curious and self-deprecating. By OotP it becomes volcanic and self-critical simultaneously. In HBP and DH it deepens into a complex of grief, obsession, and moral stubbornness. The full character is not reducible to any single book: the self-discipline of PoA Harry, the volcanic self-awareness of OotP Harry, and the morally complex obsession-prone Harry of DH together constitute the complete portrait. Critically, the interior monologue — the sardonic observations, the private shame, the grief spirals, the self-correction — is the single most important vehicle for his personality across the series.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: Daniel Radcliffe's performance preserves the most visible surface traits consistently across all eight films: bravery, loyalty, directness, moral defiance, emotional intensity, and a dry wit in the right circumstances. The dominant personality markers — courage under extreme duress, fierce protectiveness of friends, refusal to bow to Voldemort or unjust authority — are present and convincingly rendered in every film. Key individual moments are preserved with high fidelity: the 'not Slytherin' whisper (PS), the hillside identity crisis (CoS), the Patronus self-realization (PoA), the graveyard defiance (GoF), the 'It was murder' in Umbridge's class (OotP), the 'there's no need to call me sir' wit (HBP), the Elder Wand destruction (DH). These moments collectively confirm that the core personality is intact across the adaptation.
personality_voice.difference: The consistent, series-wide loss is the interior life. The self-interrogating, self-doubting, sardonic, privately grieving inner voice that is available to readers across all seven books is systematically unavailable in film form and is not adequately compensated for by behavioral equivalents. This affects different dimensions of personality differently by book — in OotP it removes the honest self-examination beneath the rage; in DH it removes the Hallows obsession as a sustained psychological state; in PoA it removes the attraction to his own trauma; in HBP it removes the grief for Sirius as a motivating undercurrent — but the cumulative effect is a Harry who is consistently more reactive and less internally complex than his book counterpart. A secondary consistent loss is specific secondary traits: the strategic self-discipline (PoA, Vernon blackmail), the pettiness and private spite (CoS, GoF), and the specific emotional granularity of his shame and self-correction (OotP, DH). The most individually damaging personality loss is the OotP self-examination register, because OotP is the book in which Harry is most morally complex and the film most flatly renders him as reactive-angry.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven book-film pairs
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The dominant personality traits are intact and consistently rendered across eight films. This prevents a severe penalty. But the interior voice — which constitutes a major dimension of the character, not a minor one — is systematically absent and not compensated. The losses are not equally distributed: OotP and DH are the most significant personality losses (self-examination and obsession arc respectively), while PS and CoS are relatively well-preserved. A weighted synthesis places the score at 19/25: dominant traits intact, secondary traits and the entire interior register reduced, with the most important books for personality (OotP, DH) showing the most significant simplification.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Harry is the primary narrative agent throughout all seven books. He initiates, investigates, decides, confronts, and drives every major plot sequence. The specific texture of his agency varies: in early books it is more reactive-heroic; in OotP and HBP it involves sustained independent investigation and strategic planning; in DH it involves a series of morally complex choices under conditions of crisis. Key acts of agency include: the Stone extraction via the mirror (PS), the Chamber confrontation (CoS), the Pettigrew mercy decision and Patronus self-realization (PoA), the graveyard defiance and Cedric warning (GoF), leading the DA and the Ministry expedition (OotP), extracting Slughorn's memory and pursuing Malfoy (HBP), the walk into the forest and Elder Wand destruction (DH). In aggregate, Harry is the undisputed structural driver of the entire series.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: Harry retains his central protagonist status and narrative driving function across all eight films. The major acts of agency in every film are preserved: Stone extraction (PS), Chamber battle (CoS), Pettigrew mercy (PoA), graveyard defiance (GoF), DA and Ministry leadership (OotP), Slughorn memory extraction (HBP), forest walk and Elder Wand destruction (DH). No film transfers Harry's primary narrative function to another character. Daniel Radcliffe's Harry is consistently the one who makes the decisive choices at key turning points.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Agency is reduced in recurring, consistent ways across the adaptation. Most significantly: investigative agency is repeatedly compressed or distributed. In PS, the Snape-wound investigation is reduced. In CoS, the Basilisk deduction is slightly collaborative. In PoA, the Pettigrew map-tracking is truncated. In GoF, the gillyweed solution is delivered by Neville rather than earned through research. In HBP, the sustained Kreacher/Dobby surveillance operation is entirely absent. In DH, the Kreacher kindness as a deliberate moral act is compressed to a transaction. The pattern is consistent: Harry's independent investigative and strategic agency — his capacity to devise and execute plans independently — is repeatedly reduced in favour of more reactive heroism. This is not a random compression; it consistently removes the evidence that Harry is a strategic thinker as well as a courageous actor.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven book-film pairs
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The central narrative function is intact. The decisive acts of agency at major turning points are preserved. The penalty is for consistent reduction of investigative and strategic agency across the series — not a single large transfer, but a cumulative pattern of small transfers that together meaningfully reduce the degree to which Harry is shown as a thinker and planner rather than merely a doer. The most significant individual agency loss is GoF's gillyweed transfer (Neville simply provides it, removing any evidence of Harry's research effort). The Kreacher/Dobby operation in HBP is also a notable loss. Score: 16/20.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Harry's motivations across the series operate on at least three levels simultaneously in every book: a primary stated motivation (destroy Voldemort, protect friends, assert truth), a secondary personal motivation (longing for family, grief for the dead, desire for belonging), and a specific internal conflict that is different in each book (dementor attraction in PoA, 'saving-people thing' in OotP, Half-Blood Prince attachment in HBP, Hallows obsession in DH). The secondary and tertiary layers are what make Harry's motivations complex rather than archetypal. Crucially, the internal conflicts are not always flattering: Harry is sometimes motivated by pride, jealousy, resentment, or obsession — and the books are explicit about this.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: Primary motivations are consistently preserved across all films: Harry's desire to fight Voldemort, protect his friends, and assert truth are all clearly rendered. The personal motivations are present but thinned: longing for family (PS, DH), grief for lost figures (OotP, HBP, DH), and desire for belonging are all indicated but not developed across time the way the books do. The specific internal conflicts are present but consistently compressed: the dementor attraction is absent (PoA), the 'saving-people thing' is named but not dramatized as causing catastrophe (OotP), the Half-Blood Prince attachment is a minor note (HBP), the Hallows obsession is present but not sustained (DH).
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The consistent loss across all films is the tertiary layer: the specific, book-unique internal conflict that gives each installment its distinctive psychological texture. In every book there is a conflict that is uncomfortable, not heroically flattering, and sustained over time — and in every film this conflict is either absent or compressed to the point where it no longer registers as a characterisation-building element. The most significant losses are: the dementor attraction (PoA — entirely absent), the full Sirius grief as motivating undercurrent (HBP — largely absent), the Hallows obsession as a genuine psychological state occupying weeks (DH — compressed to scenes), and the full anguish over Dumbledore withholding information (OotP — simplified to generic frustration).
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven book-film pairs
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Primary motivations are correctly rendered across the series. Secondary motivations are present but thinned. Tertiary/specific internal conflicts are consistently absent or compressed in every single film — this is a systematic rather than occasional loss. The fact that every film loses the uncomfortable, book-specific internal conflict that makes Harry's motivations complex rather than archetypal warrants a consistent penalty. Score: 11/15.

character_arc.book_baseline: Harry's series-long arc moves from a child with no identity, belonging, or power (PS) through escalating crisis and growing competence (CoS-GoF), through the deepest moral and psychological complexity in the series (OotP — the flawed, self-destructive hero who causes his own worst loss), through a mentorship-to-independence transition (HBP), and culminates in the freely chosen self-sacrifice of DH — the fullest expression of the series' central theme that love and choice matter more than power or fate. Within this series arc, each book has an individual arc that contributes specific development. The most important individual arcs for the overall series are: OotP (Harry as flawed hero who causes catastrophe and is sobered), HBP (Harry transitions from protected student to independent war leader), and DH (Harry moves from dependence on Dumbledore's plan to autonomous moral choice). PS establishes the foundation; CoS deepens the identity question; PoA introduces the Patronus/mastery arc and mercy as a defining trait; GoF introduces traumatized maturity.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The series-long arc is broadly preserved: Harry moves from obscure child to chosen hero to self-sacrificing victor. The major arc beats across the series are all present in correct sequence: identity discovery (PS), identity crisis and values-choice (CoS), mercy and mastery (PoA), traumatized maturity (GoF), flawed heroism and loss (OotP), mentorship transfer (HBP), self-sacrifice (DH). The series ends at the correct destination — Harry as an adult who chose freely, who survived by walking toward death, who broke the Elder Wand.
character_arc.difference: The arcs that are most compressed or damaged are precisely the most important ones for the series. OotP's arc is the most damaged: the office-destruction scene (emotional climax of the exclusion arc, theatrically cut), the Pensieve aftermath (identity crisis about James), and the ending's conversion from grief-and-hard-truth to qualified hope together mean Harry's most important single-book arc — the one that makes him a flawed, responsible adult — is only partially rendered. HBP's arc loses the explicit Ginny breakup (showing Harry choosing mission over personal happiness) and the full intellectual development through Pensieve memories. DH's arc loses the regression phase of the Hallows obsession, making the recovery at Dobby's death feel less earned. The consistent pattern is that arc low points and their corresponding earned recoveries are compressed or cut — leaving the arcs feeling more linear and heroic than the books' more regressive, crisis-ridden trajectories.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven book-film pairs
character_arc.penalty_logic: The series-long arc reaches its correct destination and its major turning points are preserved. The penalty is for consistent compression of arc low points and their earned recoveries, and for the specific damage to OotP's arc — which is the most important single-book arc contribution to the series and is the most incompletely rendered. The arc exists, is recognizable, and ends correctly. But important steps are consistently missing or rushed, and the most important arc (OotP) is tonally and structurally altered. Score: 11/15.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Harry's key relationships across the series are: (1) Dumbledore — the central mentorship, deepening into painful distance (OotP), intimate knowledge transfer (HBP), and posthumous reconciliation (DH); (2) Ron and Hermione — the trio, with textured tension, genuine mutual dependence, and Harry's specific role as emotional mediator and loyal anchor; (3) Sirius — the closest thing to a parent, source of his most acute grief after GoF; (4) Snape — sustained mutual loathing with a revelatory posthumous reconciliation; (5) Ginny — a genuine romantic relationship Harry sacrifices for duty; (6) the Weasley family as surrogate family; (7) specific book-unique relationships (Lupin in PoA, Slughorn in HBP). The quality of these relationships across the series is what gives Harry's loyalty and grief their emotional weight.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The core relational dynamics are preserved across the films. The Dumbledore-Harry bond, the trio dynamic, the Snape revelation, and the Weasley family warmth are all functional and emotionally recognizable in each film. Several individual relationship moments are excellently rendered: the Dumbledore cave sequence (HBP), the Sirius Grimmauld Place conversation (OotP), the Snape Pensieve (DH), the trio's tent dance (DH). No relationship is fundamentally reversed or transferred to another character.
key_relationships.difference: The most consistent relational loss across the series is the Sirius relationship. Sirius is Harry's most important adult relationship in GoF and OotP, and both films drastically reduce his screen time and emotional depth — GoF reduces the relationship to two brief scenes, OotP loses the full reckoning of Sirius as an irresponsible adult and Harry's complicated protectiveness. A secondary consistent loss is the Dumbledore relationship: across HBP and OotP, the specific texture of Harry's personalised resentment of Dumbledore — what makes it not generic frustration but a specific wound about being left unprotected — is consistently underplayed. The Ginny relationship loses its explicit sacrificial dimension in HBP (breakup cut). The Snape relationship loses the prophecy backstory revelation in HBP that would have given Harry's hatred its full, horrific foundation. These are not individually catastrophic but are consistent across the most emotionally important relationships.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven book-film pairs
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationships are functionally present and no major relationship is fundamentally distorted. The penalty is for consistent compression of the specific emotional textures that make each relationship more than functional: the Sirius relationship's full weight (GoF, OotP), the Dumbledore relationship's specific personalised resentment (OotP, HBP), the Ginny sacrificial dimension (HBP), and the Snape-prophecy revelation (HBP). These are meaningful losses distributed across the most important relationships. Score: 7/10.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Across the series, the book Harry is notable for specific, uncomfortable complexities that distinguish him from a generic hero: his attraction to his own trauma (PoA dementor effect), his capacity for strategic self-discipline under sustained pressure (PoA, Aunt Marge week), his small-scale moral ambiguity and pettiness (CoS, GoF), his 'saving-people thing' as a flaw that directly causes catastrophe (OotP), his Hallows obsession as weeks of irrational passivity and poor leadership (DH), his cruelty to Lupin (DH), his capacity for resentment sustained over time (OotP anger, DH Dumbledore fury), his deliberate moral choices in relationships (Kreacher kindness, DH), and the specific texture of his mistakes and failures that make his eventual choices feel earned rather than generic. This complexity is not evenly distributed — it peaks in OotP and DH.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve the most visible and plot-essential complexity: the mercy decisions (PoA, DH), the moral uses of dark magic (DH Imperius Curse), the self-sacrifice as free choice rather than compulsion (DH), the identity crisis across multiple books, and the emotional vulnerability in key scenes. The Sectumsempra horror (HBP), the graveyard defiance rooted in pride as much as courage (GoF), and the Dumbledore resentment (DH) are all present.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The consistent, series-wide loss is the material that makes Harry specifically uncomfortable and morally complex rather than heroically troubled. The losses that matter most in aggregate: the dementor attraction (PoA — entirely absent), the Aunt Marge sustained self-discipline (PoA — absent), the pettiness and spite (CoS, GoF — internal, unavailable), the 'saving-people thing' as directly causing Sirius's death (OotP — present but not dramatized as self-inflicted catastrophe), the Hallows obsession as weeks of genuine moral compromise (DH — compressed), the Lupin cruelty (DH — theatrical cut), the Kreacher deliberate kindness (DH — compressed to transaction), the Sirius grief as motivating undercurrent (HBP — largely absent), and the specific Half-Blood Prince attachment (HBP — minor note). These collectively convert a character who is sometimes passive, sometimes wrong, sometimes cruel, and sustained in doubt — into a character who is troubled but fundamentally on a heroic course.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven book-film pairs
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This dimension shows the most consistent series-wide pattern of loss. In every single book, meaningful nuance and specific complexity are absent or compressed to the point of non-registration. The character is not reduced to a single trait — enough complexity survives to prevent a lower score — but the specific, uncomfortable, non-heroic complexities that make him a fully realised person rather than a well-executed protagonist archetype are systematically removed. The losses are heaviest in OotP and DH, which are also the books where this complexity is most important. Score: 9/15.

score_caps_applied: No hard cap applied. The score of 73 reflects weighted synthesis rather than a cap. The most important books for Harry's overall arc (OotP, DH, HBP) show the most significant losses, and this weighting pulls the synthesis below the average of per-book scores (75.0). OotP is the single most damaging book for the adaptation's fidelity, particularly in arc and complexity, and its centrality to Harry's character development as a flawed, self-aware adult is weighted heavily.
comparative.key_observations: The synthesis score of 73 sits slightly below the arithmetic mean of the per-book scores (75.0), reflecting a deliberate weighting toward the books most important to Harry's overall characterisation. The films succeed consistently and convincingly at the most visible layer of Harry's character: Daniel Radcliffe's performance preserves bravery, loyalty, moral defiance, directness, and emotional intensity across all eight films, and the major narrative turning points — Stone extraction, Chamber battle, Patronus, graveyard, DA leadership, cave sequence, forest walk — are all faithfully rendered. This prevents the score from falling into the 60s. The consistent penalty across all six dimensions reflects a systematic rather than occasional failure: the interior life is unavailable by medium and not compensated; investigative and strategic agency is repeatedly compressed in favour of reactive heroism; specific internal conflicts are present but rarely sustained long enough to register as characterisation-building; arc low points are consistently compressed, making recoveries feel less earned; key relationships lose their specific emotional textures rather than their functional presence; and the uncomfortable, non-heroic complexities that most distinguish book Harry are systematically absent. The single most damaging adaptation decision across the entire series is the theatrical cut of OotP's office-destruction scene, which removes the emotional climax of Harry's most important individual arc. The second most damaging is the DH compression of the Hallows obsession, which converts weeks of genuine moral compromise into a few scenes of manageable doubt. The result is a Harry who is recognisably, substantially the same character across eight films — but who is a cleaner, more linear, more reactive hero than the morally complex, self-interrogating, sometimes wrong, sometimes cruel, grief-ridden person the books spent seven volumes constructing.
